derivations.claim: Universal models and their specified contractions. Let $Q_{p,r}$ be the free bisimplicial $R$-module whose value at $(p',r')$ is the free module $R[\Delta([p'],[p])\times\Delta([r'],[r])]$ on pairs of monotone maps; the Yoneda bijection $\operatorname{Hom}(Q_{p,r},M)\cong M_{p,r}$ sends a bisimplicial map to the image of the generator $(\mathrm{id}_{[p]},\mathrm{id}_{[r]})$. Under this bijection the diagonal alternating-face complex of $Q_{p,r}$ is the free simplicial $R$-module on the product of standard simplices $\Delta[p]\times\Delta[r]$, a chain complex in the sense of [F4], and the double total complex of $Q_{p,r}$ is the tensor product $C_*(\Delta[p];R)\otimes_RC_*(\Delta[r];R)$ of the two Moore complexes with the Koszul differential, which is the direct-sum total complex of [F3]. Each of the two complexes carries a specified contraction $H$ with $\partial H+H\partial=\mathrm{id}-\iota\varepsilon$ onto the vertex $\omega$: on the diagonal model, $(\alpha,\beta,t)\mapsto(\max(\alpha,tp),\max(\beta,tr))$ is a simplicial homotopy of $\Delta[p]\times\Delta[r]\times\Delta[1]$ from the identity to the constant map at $\omega$, and the prism formula of [F1] turns it into a chain homotopy from the identity to the constant chain map $\iota\varepsilon$; on the tensor product, $H(x\otimes y)=h_p(x)\otimes y+e(x)\otimes h_r(y)$, where $h_p,h_r$ are the two prism homotopies and $e=\iota\varepsilon$ is the vertex projector supported in degree zero, satisfies $\partial H+H\partial=\mathrm{id}-e\otimes e$ by direct expansion, because $e\partial=0$ kills the two cross terms and the remaining Koszul signs cancel. In both models every cycle of positive degree, and every degree-zero cycle annihilated by $\varepsilon$, is the boundary of its specified image under $H$. [F1, F3, F4, construct]

A natural map from the diagonal total to the double total. For each $m\geq0$ the degree-$m$ parts are $\operatorname{Diag}_m(M)=M_{m,m}$ and $\operatorname{Tot}_m(M)=\bigoplus_{p+r=m}M_{p,r}$, direct sums of representable functors; by Yoneda, natural maps $\varphi_m:\operatorname{Diag}_m\to\operatorname{Tot}_m$ are exactly choices of elements $c_m\in\operatorname{Tot}_m(Q_{m,m})$, namely their values on the universal elements $\mathrm{id}\in M_{m,m}$, a general element $x\in M_{m,m}$ being sent to the image of $c_m$ under its representing map $\tilde x:Q_{m,m}\to M$. Set $c_0$ equal to the generator of $(Q_{0,0})_{0,0}$; since $\operatorname{Diag}_0(M)=M_{0,0}=\operatorname{Tot}_0(M)$, this forces $\varphi_0=\mathrm{id}$. For $m\geq1$, having constructed $\varphi_{m-1}$ with $\partial\varphi_{m-1}=\varphi_{m-2}\partial$, put $b_m:=\varphi_{m-1}(\delta_{\mathrm{diag}}\,\mathrm{id})\in\operatorname{Tot}_{m-1}(Q_{m,m})$ and $c_m:=H_m(b_m)$, the contraction of step 1.1 applied to the positive-degree cycle $b_m$; for $m=1$ the element $b_1\in(Q_{1,1})_{0,0}$ is $(\omega_1,\omega_1)-(\omega_0,\omega_0)$, whose two vertex coefficients cancel under $\varepsilon$, so step 1.1 applies there as well. Then $\partial c_m=b_m$ and the induced natural maps satisfy $\partial\varphi_m=\varphi_{m-1}\partial$: on the universal element this is $\partial c_m=b_m$, and for general $x$ naturality of $\varphi_{m-1}$ and functoriality of the representing maps give $\partial\varphi_m(x)=\tilde x_*(\partial c_m)=\tilde x_*(b_m)=\varphi_{m-1}(\tilde x_*(\partial\,\mathrm{id}))=\varphi_{m-1}(\partial x)$, with $\varphi_m$ additive and natural because $x\mapsto\tilde x$ is $R$-linear and natural. [step 1.1, construct]

A natural map in the reverse direction. On the $(p,r)$-summand of $\operatorname{Tot}_m$ with $p+r=m$, natural maps $M_{p,r}\to M_{m,m}$ correspond by Yoneda to elements $c'_{p,r}\in\operatorname{Diag}_m(Q_{p,r})=(Q_{p,r})_{m,m}$, and a general element of $M_{p,r}$ is sent to the image of $c'_{p,r}$ under its representing map. Set $c'_{0,0}$ equal to the generator; for $m\geq1$ and each such $(p,r)$, having constructed $\psi_{m-1}$ with $\partial\psi_{m-1}=\psi_{m-2}\partial$, put $b'_{p,r}:=\psi_{m-1}(\partial\,\mathrm{id})\in\operatorname{Diag}_{m-1}(Q_{p,r})$, where $\partial\,\mathrm{id}$ is the boundary of the universal $(p,r)$-element in the total complex of $Q_{p,r}$, and $c'_{p,r}:=H'_m(b'_{p,r})$ for the diagonal contraction of step 1.1 on $Q_{p,r}$. As in step 2.1, $\partial b'_{p,r}=0$ by the induction hypothesis, and for $m=1$ the two summands $(p,r)=(1,0),(0,1)$ have $b'_{p,r}$ of degree zero with vertex coefficients cancelling, so in all cases $\partial c'_{p,r}=b'_{p,r}$; the induced maps satisfy $\partial\psi_m=\psi_{m-1}\partial$ by the same representing-map computation, and are additive and natural. [step 1.1, construct]

Homotopies between natural maps agreeing in degree zero, and the inverse identities. Let $F,F':C\to C'$ be natural chain maps between complexes whose degree parts are finite direct sums of representable functors $M\mapsto M_{p,r}$ or $M\mapsto M_{m,m}$, and suppose $F_0=F'_0$. Define natural maps $h_m:C_m\to C'_{m+1}$ by recursion: on a universal element $z$ of a representing summand of $C_m$, the element $\beta_m:=(F_m-F'_m)(z)-\partial h_{m-1}(\partial z)\in C'_m(Q)$ has $\partial\beta_m=(F-F')_{m-1}\partial z-\partial h_{m-1}\partial z=h_{m-2}\partial\partial z=0$, using $\partial h_{m-1}+h_{m-2}\partial=F-F'$ in degree $m-1$, so it is a cycle in a model complex $C'(Q)$ that is either a total or a diagonal model of step 1.1; set $h_m(z):=H(\beta_m)$ for $m\geq1$ and $h_0:=0$, fillings that are specified and linear, and extend by the representing maps. Then $\partial h_m+h_{m-1}\partial=F-F'$ holds in every degree by construction and by naturality. Taking $C=C'=\operatorname{Diag}$ and $F=\psi\varphi$, $F'=\mathrm{id}$, whose degree-zero parts are both the identity, gives $\psi\varphi\simeq\mathrm{id}$; taking $C=C'=\operatorname{Tot}$ and $F=\varphi\psi$, $F'=\mathrm{id}$ gives $\varphi\psi\simeq\mathrm{id}$. Hence $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are natural chain-homotopy equivalences inverse to each other. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct]

Cosimplicial variance and an internal differential. Two formal extensions. (a) Every formula and identity of steps 1.1-3.1 is a finite $R$-linear combination of composites of structure operators, together with the explicit model fillings; equivalently, each identity is an identity between such combinations in the free additive category generated by the simplex category. Reversing every arrow turns the simplicial identities into the cosimplicial identities and preserves each identity term by term, so the same construction compares the total complex of horizontal and vertical coface operators with its diagonal total. (b) Suppose in addition that an endomorphism $d$ squares to zero and commutes with every structure operator, as for the internal degree $q\geq a$ of the Statement; perform the construction family-wise in $q$. The formulas involve no $d$, so each constructed map commutes with $d$, and the displayed sign twists are exactly the ones tracked by the bidegree: $\varphi,\psi$ preserve $p+r$, so on their images $(-1)^{p+r}=(-1)^n$; the homotopies raise $p+r$ by one, so the internal contributions to $\partial H+H\partial$ are $(-1)^{p+r}Hd+(-1)^{p+r+1}dH=(-1)^{p+r}(Hd-dH)=0$. Thus the identities of steps 2.1-3.1 lift verbatim to the differentials $\delta_h+(-1)^p\delta_v+(-1)^{p+r}d$ and $\delta_{\mathrm{diag}}+(-1)^nd$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

Finiteness, normalization, augmentation and derived presentations. Since $K^{p,r,q}=0$ unless $p,r\geq0$ and $q\geq a$, in each total degree $m$ only finitely many summands occur, on both sides; every constructed map and homotopy is a finite sum over such summands, so [F2] permits using either total notation and no dimension hypothesis on the coefficient modules is needed. All fillers are specified values of explicit contractions built from face and degeneracy operators, so no choice principle is used. Since $\varphi_0=\psi_0=\mathrm{id}$ and $h_0=0$, the comparisons preserve the augmentation. By [F1] the normalization inclusion is a natural chain homotopy equivalence; applying it on the diagonal side, or in either simplicial direction of the total, and composing with the comparison of steps 2.1-3.1 gives natural chain homotopy equivalences between any mixture of normalized and unnormalized totalizations, so normalization may be applied on either side. A supplied functorial strict resolution presents a coherent derived diagram by strict bicosimplicial complexes; the comparison is natural in the coefficient diagram, hence compatible with the resolution maps, independent of the chosen presentation, and descends to a natural isomorphism of the derived objects. [F1, F2, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1] ∎

derivations.claim: Bounded strict model and finite diagonals. Choose a cochain lower bound $a$ with $F$ represented by a strict complex vanishing in degrees $q<a$, possible because $F$ is cohomologically bounded; by [F1] exact inverse image preserves vanishing there, so the same $a$ bounds every $F_p$, and right-derived pushforward produces a functorial double model in degrees $p\geq0$, $q\geq a$. In total degree $m$ only $0\leq p\leq m-a$ occurs, so every diagonal is finite and [F2]'s strict total model may be used with either totalization. Take the cone of the augmented map $F\to\operatorname{Tot}_pRf_{p*}F_p$, place the augmentation in column $p=-1$, and filter by $p$; each total degree of the cone involves only finitely many columns. At a point $x\in X$ the stalk of the cone is the cone of the stalk map, and because the stalk functor is exact and commutes with the finite column sums, this stalk carries the induced finite filtration, whose first page in internal degree $q$ is the augmented horizontal row of $H^q$ of the stalk complexes. [F1, F2, given]

The stalk row and one chosen point. Fix $x\in X$ and put $K=F_x$, a complex of $k$-vector spaces with $H^q(K)=H^q(F)_x$; surjectivity of $f$ makes the fiber $S=Y_x$ nonempty. By the proper base change and fiber-pullback clauses of [F1], the stalk at $x$ of $Rf_{p*}F_p$ is $R\Gamma(S^{p+1},K)$ with $K$ the constant derived pullback, and these identifications are natural for all face and degeneracy maps, so the first page of the stalk row in internal degree $q$ is
$$H^q(K)\xrightarrow{\delta_{-1}}H^q(S,K)\xrightarrow{\delta_0}H^q(S^2,K)\xrightarrow{\delta_1}\cdots,$$
where $\delta_p$ is the alternating sum of the pullbacks along the $(p+2)$ coordinate-deletion maps $d_i:S^{p+2}\to S^{p+1}$. Choose one point $y\in S$; no assertion that any positive cohomology group of $S$ vanishes, or that $S$ is connected or smooth, is made or used. [F1, A1, step 1.1]

Explicit contraction of every augmented row. For $r\geq0$ let $\mathrm{ins}_r:S^r\to S^{r+1}$ insert $y$ as first coordinate, with $S^0=\mathrm{pt}$; so $\mathrm{ins}_0$ is the point $y$ itself. The deletion and insertion maps satisfy $d_0\,\mathrm{ins}_{r+1}=\mathrm{id}$ and $d_i\,\mathrm{ins}_{r+1}=\mathrm{ins}_r\,d_{i-1}$ for $i>0$. Put $h_{p+1}:=\mathrm{ins}_{p+1}^*:H^q(S^{p+2},K)\to H^q(S^{p+1},K)$ and $h_0:=\mathrm{ins}_0^*:H^q(S,K)\to H^q(K)$, with $\delta_{-1}$ the constant pullback of the projection $S\to\mathrm{pt}$. Applying the two identities termwise gives $h_{p+1}\delta_p+\delta_{p-1}h_p=\mathrm{id}$ for every $p\geq0$: the $i=0$ term of $h_{p+1}\delta_p$ is the identity, and the terms $i>0$ are the negatives of $\delta_{p-1}h_p$; moreover $h_0\delta_{-1}=\mathrm{id}$, because the projection followed by the chosen point is the identity of $\mathrm{pt}$. Hence every augmented horizontal row is contractible, in particular exact, in every internal degree $q$, using only functorial pullback on cohomology. [step 1.2, algebra]

Conclusion and naturality. By step 2.1 the next page of the spectral sequence of the stalk cone vanishes at every stalk, and by step 1.1 its filtration is finite in each total degree, so [F3] identifies the associated graded of the stalk cohomology with zero in every degree; the stalk of the cone at $x$ is therefore acyclic, for every $x\in X$. A complex of sheaves whose stalks are all acyclic has zero cohomology sheaves, hence is acyclic; this proves the asserted quasi-isomorphism $F\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Tot}_{p\geq0}Rf_{p*}F_p$. All algebraic base changes of $f$ remain proper surjective, and the identifications of steps 1.2-3.1 are pullbacks of one another by the Cartesian-pasting naturality of [F1], so the pulled-back assertion follows without choosing compatible points; coefficient morphisms act componentwise by the same naturality. Applying the derived global-section functor, which preserves the finite direct sums forming each total degree and satisfies $R\Gamma(X,Rf_{p*}F_p)\cong R\Gamma(Y_p,F_p)$ by the composition clause of [F1], gives $R\Gamma(X,F)\simeq\operatorname{Tot}_pR\Gamma(Y_p,F_p)$. The Axiom of Choice is inherited exactly through [A1]. [F1, F3, A1, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

Let $f:Y\to X$ be a proper surjective morphism of finite-type complex algebraic varieties, and let $F\in D^b_c(X;k)$ for a field $k$. Write $Y_p=Y\times_X\cdots\times_XY$ with $p+1$ factors, $f_p:Y_p\to X$, and $F_p=f_p^*F$. In the analytic topology of [[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]] the natural augmented derived Cech map is a quasi-isomorphism:
$$F\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Tot}_{p\geq0}Rf_{p*}F_p.$$
Here totalization is the normalized or unnormalized alternating-face total supplied by the simplicial-derived construction. There is one fixed lower cochain bound; consequently its diagonals are finite in every degree. The claim commutes with arbitrary algebraic base change and coefficient morphisms. In particular $R\Gamma(X,F)\simeq\operatorname{Tot}_pR\Gamma(Y_p,F_p)$. Individual fibers of $f$ need not be cohomologically acyclic, connected, or smooth.

For a bicosimplicial complex $K^{p,r,q}$ of modules over a commutative ring, with $p,r\geq0$ and one fixed lower bound $q\geq a$, the alternating-face total complex and the diagonal alternating-face total complex are naturally chain-homotopy equivalent:
$$\operatorname{Tot}_{p,r,q}K^{p,r,q}\simeq\operatorname{Tot}_{n,q}K^{n,n,q}.$$
On the left total degree is $p+r+q$ and differential is $\delta_h+(-1)^p\delta_v+(-1)^{p+r}d$; on the right total degree is $n+q$ and differential is $\delta_{\mathrm{diag}}+(-1)^nd$. They require no dimensional finiteness of the coefficient modules and no choice principle. Normalization can be applied on either side without changing the conclusion.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Height zero and the induction setup. Let $U\to X$ be a bounded proper hypercover of height zero, that is $U=\operatorname{cosk}_0U_0$. By the convention of the Given, $U$ is the Cech nerve of the proper surjection $U_0\to X$, so [F1] proves both the sheaf and the global augmentation statements for $U$. Suppose inductively that they are proved for all bounded proper hypercovers of height at most $n$, and let $U=\operatorname{cosk}_{n+1}U$ have height $n+1$. Put $V:=\operatorname{cosk}_nU$. Its matching maps through degree $n$ are those of $U$, and in degrees $j>n$ its matching map is an isomorphism because $V=\operatorname{cosk}_nV$; hence $V$ is a proper hypercover of height at most $n$ and the induction hypothesis applies to $V$.

Levelwise proper surjectivity of $U\to V$. For every $j$ the map $U_j\to V_j$ is proper surjective. For $j\leq n$ it is the identity. For $j>n$ it reads $\operatorname{Hom}(\operatorname{sk}_{n+1}\Delta[j],U)\to\operatorname{Hom}(\operatorname{sk}_n\Delta[j],U)$: the domain is obtained from the codomain by adjoining the finitely many nondegenerate $(n+1)$-faces of $\Delta[j]$, whose boundaries already lie in the $n$-skeleton, so this map is a Cartesian pullback of the finite product of the matching map $U_{n+1}\to(\operatorname{cosk}_nU)_{n+1}=V_{n+1}$; a finite product over $X$ of proper surjections, and any base change of it, is proper surjective. No local sections are required, and all limits are the finite matching limits of the Given.

The bisimplicial Cech model and the double total. Form the bisimplicial object $W_{r,j}=U_j\times_{V_j}\cdots\times_{V_j}U_j$ with $r+1$ factors, horizontally the Cech nerve of $U_j\to V_j$, and pull coefficients from $X$ throughout. By [F1] and step 1.2, for each fixed $j$ the horizontally augmented derived row computes the coefficient complex on $V_j$, before and after pushing forward to $X$: with $B_j:=(V_j\to X)^*F$ and $a_{r,j}:W_{r,j}\to X$ one has $Rb_{j*}B_j\simeq\operatorname{Tot}_rRa_{r,j*}a_{r,j}^*F$, where $b_j:V_j\to X$, the identifications being compatible with composition and finite sums by [F3] and [F4]. The induction hypothesis for $V$ gives $F\simeq\operatorname{Tot}_jRb_{j*}B_j$; substituting the row identifications and using that every total diagonal is finite (the internal degrees are bounded below by the same $a$, by [F3]) identifies the iterated total with the full total, so $F\simeq\operatorname{Tot}_{r,j}Ra_{r,j*}a_{r,j}^*F$ and the analogous global statement hold. By [F2] this double total is naturally chain-homotopy equivalent to the total on the diagonal $D_j:=W_{j,j}$.

The retract over $X$. The bounded hypercover $U$ is a retract over $X$ of $D$. The map $i:U\to D$ repeats the same $U_j$-point in all $j+1$ horizontal factors, the horizontal degeneracy; through degree $n$ the map $U_j\to V_j$ is the identity, so $D_j=U_j$ there, and in degree $n+1$ let $r_{n+1}:D_{n+1}\to U_{n+1}$ be the projection to the first horizontal factor. Its faces and degeneracies agree with the degree-$\leq n$ identity identifications, because every horizontal factor of $W$ has the same image in $V$ and the lower-degree maps are identities; this defines a map of $(n+1)$-truncated simplicial objects over $X$, and the universal property $U=\operatorname{cosk}_{n+1}U$ extends it uniquely to $r:D\to U$. The composite $ri$ is the identity through degree $n+1$: in lower degrees because $i$ is the diagonal and $r$ the factor projection on $D_j=U_j$, and in degree $n+1$ because repeating a point and projecting a factor returns it; hence $ri=\mathrm{id}$ in every degree by the same universal property. Coefficient pullback reverses these maps, and since $r\circ i=\mathrm{id}$ the augmented total of $U$ is a retract of the augmented total of $D$; by step 2.1 the cone of the augmentation of $D$ is acyclic, and a retract of an acyclic cone is acyclic, so the augmentation of $U$ is a quasi-isomorphism. This completes the bounded-height induction.

Arbitrary height by truncation. For an arbitrary proper hypercover $U$, put $U^{(N)}:=\operatorname{cosk}_N\operatorname{sk}_NU$; it is a bounded proper hypercover, so step 3.1 applies to it, and the canonical map $U\to U^{(N)}$ is the identity through simplicial degree $N$. In the strict derived total model every internal degree is at least $a$; hence total degrees $m-1$, $m$ and $m+1$ involve only simplicial levels $p\leq m-a+1$, because a term of total degree $m+1$ has $p+q=m+1$ with $q\geq a$. Choose $N\geq\max(0,m-a+1)$; then the totals for $U$ and $U^{(N)}$ have the same objects and the same differentials in these three degrees, so the same degree-$m$ cohomology and the same augmentation maps. Since $m$ was arbitrary, the augmentation for $U$ is a quasi-isomorphism, and degree $m$ with its differential is determined by levels through $p=m-a+1$. This is a finite-degree truncation argument, not an interchange of stalks or cohomology with an unjustified infinite product.

The spectral sequence and convergence. Filter the global total of step 4.1 by simplicial degree. Its first page is $E_1^{p,q}=H^q(X_p,a_p^*F)$, with first differential the alternating sum of face pullbacks by the naturality of [F3]; in degree $m$ the filtration has only the finitely many pieces $0\leq p\leq m-a$. By [F5] the stationary page is identified, naturally, with the finite associated graded of $H^m(X,F)$; this proves strong convergence and requires no finite-dimensionality of the individual groups $H^q(X_p,a_p^*F)$.

Refinements and constant coefficients. For two proper hypercovers $U,V$ of $X$, the levelwise product $R_j:=U_j\times_XV_j$ is a proper hypercover: finite matching limits commute with products, so each matching map of $R$ is the product over $X$ of the matching maps of $U$ and $V$, hence proper surjective, and the levelwise projections give maps of simplicial objects $R\to U$ and $R\to V$ over $X$. By step 4.1 the augmentations of $U$, $V$ and $R$ all identify their totals with the same coefficient complex on $X$, and the refinement maps are compatible with those identifications by naturality of the augmentation, so all proper-hypercover refinements induce the same comparison via the base object. A smooth-projective refinement requires a separate supplied construction: the levelwise product of smooth morphisms over a singular base $X$ need not be smooth, so no smoothness is asserted here. For $F=k_X$ the lower bound is $a=0$ and the page of step 5.1 is exactly the stated first-quadrant spectral sequence. The Axiom of Choice is inherited precisely through [A1].

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the supplied injective-resolution six-functor construction. Let $f:Y\to X$ be a proper surjective morphism of finite-type complex algebraic varieties, and let $F\in D^b_c(X;k)$ for a field $k$. Write $Y_p=Y\times_X\cdots\times_XY$ with $p+1$ factors, $f_p:Y_p\to X$, and $F_p=f_p^*F$. In the analytic topology of [[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]] the natural augmented derived Cech map is a quasi-isomorphism:
$$F\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Tot}_{p\geq0}Rf_{p*}F_p.$$
Here totalization is the normalized or unnormalized alternating-face total supplied by the simplicial-derived construction. There is one fixed lower cochain bound; consequently its diagonals are finite in every degree. The claim commutes with arbitrary algebraic base change and coefficient morphisms. In particular $R\Gamma(X,F)\simeq\operatorname{Tot}_pR\Gamma(Y_p,F_p)$. Individual fibers of $f$ need not be cohomologically acyclic, connected, or smooth.

Fix an algebraically closed field $k$. The affine models used here are polynomial zero sets $Z\subseteq k^n$, including empty and reducible sets. Their closed subsets are common zero loci of polynomial families, relative to $Z$. Intersections combine equations, and finite unions use products of equations, so these are the closed sets of a topology.

For an open $U\subseteq Z$, let $\mathcal O_Z(U)$ consist of functions $U\to k$ locally equal to $a/b$ for polynomials $a,b$ with $b$ nonvanishing on the chosen neighbourhood. Pointwise operations and restriction make these sets a sheaf of $k$-algebras: quotient expressions persist on restriction, and functions that agree locally glue uniquely with the same local quotient property. At a point z its stalk is the ring of germs of such functions. Evaluation at z maps it onto k, with kernel the germs vanishing at z. A germ nonzero at z is invertible: shrink to where its numerator and denominator are both nonzero and interchange them. Thus the kernel is the unique maximal ideal. These affine models are locally ringed spaces in the sense of [[def-locally-ringed-space]], with residue fields canonically k.

A **classical algebraic prevariety** over k is a quasi-compact locally ringed space with a structure sheaf of k-algebras, covered by open subspaces isomorphic over k to these affine models. Here quasi-compact means every open cover has a finite subcover. Equivalently it admits a finite affine-model cover. To justify the converse, each affine model is quasi-compact: polynomial principal opens $D_Z(h)=\{z:h(z)\ne0\}$ form a basis. Given an open cover, take all h whose principal opens lie in a member. Their principal opens cover Z. The ideal generated by these h in $k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$ is finitely generated by [[thm-hilbert-basis-theorem]], iterated from the field k. Express finitely many generators using finitely many of the original h. Those finitely many h have the same common zero locus as the whole ideal, hence their principal opens still cover Z and yield a finite subcover. The empty model has the empty subcover. A finite union of quasi-compact subspaces is quasi-compact.

A map is **regular** when it is a morphism of locally ringed spaces as in [[def-morphism-locally-ringed-spaces]] whose sheaf maps respect k. For these function sheaves its sheaf map is necessarily pullback of functions: the local stalk map induces a k-map between residue fields k, hence the identity, so the value of a pulled-back section at x is its value at the image of x. Conversely, continuous pullback of local regular functions gives a local stalk map because a function vanishing at the image vanishes after pullback.

Regularity can therefore be checked on affine charts: near every source point choose a target affine chart containing its image and an open neighbourhood in a source affine chart mapped into it; the target coordinate functions must pull back to locally polynomial quotients. This condition also implies continuity. Indeed zero sets of locally polynomial quotients are locally polynomial zero sets, hence closed; pulling back polynomial equations consequently gives closed sets. Substitution then pulls every local quotient on the target back to a local quotient on the source, using this continuity to restrict to its domain and its nonvanishing denominator. Thus the chart condition and the locally ringed-space definition agree.

A prevariety is **separated** when the equalizer of every pair of regular maps into it, from any classical prevariety, is closed. A **classical algebraic variety** is a separated prevariety. Here varieties may be reducible or empty; an **irreducible classical variety** is nonempty and irreducible in the sense of [[def-irreducible-topological-space-and-subset]]. These definitions and the local verifications above use no Axiom of Choice.

Let $X$ be a classical algebraic variety over $\mathbb C$ in the sense of
[[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]: a separated
quasi-compact locally ringed space over $\mathbb C$ with a finite cover by
affine models $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, the morphisms being the regular maps,
i.e. the morphisms of locally ringed spaces over $\mathbb C$
([[def-morphism-locally-ringed-spaces]]).

(a) **Analytic topology.** An affine model $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ carries the
subspace topology of the Euclidean topology of $\mathbb C^n$
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]],
[[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]). If $Z_1,Z_2\subseteq X$ are affine
models and $\varphi:Z_1\to Z_2$ is the structure-sheaf isomorphism, then on
$Z_1\cap Z_2$ the maps $\varphi$ and $\varphi^{-1}$ are given locally by
polynomial quotient functions
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]) and are
therefore continuous for the Euclidean topologies: polynomial functions are
continuous, and a quotient is continuous wherever its denominator does not
vanish ([[lem-algebra-of-continuous-real-maps-on-a-space]],
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]). Hence the topologies transported
from the two affine models agree on the overlap, so the affine-model topologies
glue to a unique topology on the underlying set of $X$
([[def-topological-space]], [[def-subspace-topology-top]]): the **analytic
topology** of $X$. Every regular map of complex classical varieties is
continuous for the analytic topologies, by the same local description
([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and the analytic topology refines the Zariski
topology because polynomial zero sets are Euclidean closed. Whenever a complex
algebraic variety is used as a topological space below it carries the analytic
topology, and each subvariety carries the subspace topology.

(b) **Smooth points.** Let $S$ be a classical variety over $\mathbb C$ and let
$x\in S$. The point $x$ is a **smooth point of $S$** if its algebraic local ring
$\mathcal O_{S,x}$ is a regular local ring: a nonzero Noetherian local ring
whose maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_x$ satisfies
$\dim_{\mathbb C}(\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2)=\dim\mathcal O_{S,x}$
([[def-embedding-dimension-and-regular-local-ring]]). The residue field at a
classical complex point is $\mathbb C$. The variety $S$ is **smooth** if every
point is smooth. This intrinsic algebraic condition does not require a Zariski
neighbourhood to be algebraically isomorphic to an open subset of affine space.

(c) **Finite smooth algebraic stratifications.** A **finite smooth algebraic
stratification with the frontier condition** of $X$ is a finite decomposition
$X=\coprod_{\alpha\in A}S_\alpha$ into pairwise disjoint nonempty connected
locally closed subsets $S_\alpha\subseteq X$ — the **strata** — such that each
$S_\alpha$, with its reduced induced algebraic structure, is a smooth algebraic
subvariety of $X$; and such that for every $\alpha$ the closure
$\overline{S_\alpha}$ of $S_\alpha$ in $X$ is a union of strata. The latter is
the **frontier condition**: the frontier
$\overline{S_\alpha}\setminus S_\alpha$ of every stratum is a union of strata
([[def-connected-space]], [[def-interior-closure-boundary-top]]).

**The induced structure is the polynomial-quotient function sheaf, not a
restriction of $\mathcal O_X$.** A locally closed $S\subseteq X$ is, locally
inside an affine model $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, the set of points with $h\neq0$
and $f_1=\dots=f_r=0$ for polynomials $h,f_1,\dots,f_r$ on $Z$
([[def-constructible-subset-variety]],
[[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]); the map
$z\mapsto(z,1/h(z))$ identifies it with the affine model
$\{(z,t):th(z)=1,\ f_1(z)=\dots=f_r(z)=0\}\subseteq\mathbb C^{n+1}$, and its
**reduced induced structure sheaf** is the one transported along this
identification: locally functions of the form $a/b$ with $b$ nonvanishing on the
set. The ambient restriction $\mathcal O_X|_S$ is not used, since already at the
origin of the affine line the ambient stalk is the local ring of the line while
the stalk of the reduced point is $\mathbb C$. An open subset of an affine model
is a union of principal open subsets, and each principal open subset is again an
affine model, so every locally closed subvariety of $X$ is a classical variety
for the induced structure sheaf. No existence theorem for stratifications, no
common-refinement theorem and no choice principle is asserted: nothing is
selected, and all cited suppliers are choice-free.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

**A point outside $X$, named rather than assumed.** Put

$$\infty \;:=\; \{\, y \in X : y \notin y \,\},$$

a set by Separation. Then $\infty \notin X$: were $\infty \in X$, the defining
condition applied to $\infty$ itself would give
$\infty \in \infty \iff \infty \notin \infty$. So no hypothesis about $X$ is
needed to obtain a point outside it, and the construction below is available for
every space.

**The space.** Put $X^{*} := X \cup \{\infty\}$ and

$$\mathcal{T}^{*} \;:=\; \mathcal{T} \;\cup\; \{\, X^{*} \setminus C \;:\; C \subseteq X,\ C \text{ closed in } X \text{ and a compact subset of } X \,\} .$$

The pair $(X^{*}, \mathcal{T}^{*})$ is the **one-point compactification**, or
**Alexandroff compactification**, of $X$. Members of $\mathcal{T}$ are said to be
of the **first kind** and the sets $X^{*} \setminus C$ of the **second kind**; a
set of the second kind is exactly an open set of $\mathcal{T}^{*}$ containing
$\infty$, since a member of $\mathcal{T}$ is a subset of $X$, and the set $C$ is
recovered from it as $C = X^{*} \setminus (X^{*} \setminus C)$.

**$\mathcal{T}^{*}$ is a topology on $X^{*}$, and this is discharged here.**
Throughout, "closed" and "compact" without qualification mean closed in $X$ and a
compact subset of $X$ ([[def-compact-space]]); two facts about such sets are used
and both are [[thm-closed-subspace-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]: a subset of a
compact $C$ that is closed in $X$ is closed in the subspace $C$
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]) and hence compact, and a union of two compact
subsets is compact.

*(T1).* $\varnothing \in \mathcal{T}$, and $X^{*} = X^{*} \setminus \varnothing$
is of the second kind, $\varnothing$ being closed in $X$ and compact.

*(T2).* Let $\mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathcal{T}^{*}$, let $\mathcal{S}_1$ be the
members of $\mathcal{S}$ lying in $\mathcal{T}$ and $\mathcal{S}_2$ the rest, so
that every member of $\mathcal{S}_2$ is of the second kind. If
$\mathcal{S}_2 = \varnothing$ then $\bigcup \mathcal{S} = \bigcup \mathcal{S}_1$
lies in $\mathcal{T}$ by (T2) in $X$. Otherwise put
$U := \bigcup \mathcal{S}_1 \in \mathcal{T}$ and
$\mathcal{D} := \{\, X^{*} \setminus O : O \in \mathcal{S}_2 \,\}$, a nonempty
family of closed compact subsets of $X$, and $C_0 := \bigcap \mathcal{D}$. Then
$C_0$ is closed by (C2) of [[def-topological-space]], and it is a closed subset of
any one member of $\mathcal{D}$, hence compact. Now

$$\bigcup \mathcal{S} \;=\; U \cup (X^{*} \setminus C_0) \;=\; X^{*} \setminus (C_0 \setminus U),$$

and $C_0 \setminus U = C_0 \cap (X \setminus U)$ is closed in $X$ and a subset of
the compact $C_0$, hence compact; so $\bigcup \mathcal{S}$ is of the second kind.

*(T3).* For $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$ the intersection lies in $\mathcal{T}$ by (T3)
in $X$. For two sets of the second kind,
$(X^{*} \setminus C) \cap (X^{*} \setminus D) = X^{*} \setminus (C \cup D)$, and
$C \cup D$ is closed in $X$ and compact as a union of two compact subsets. For one
of each, $\infty \notin U$ gives
$U \cap (X^{*} \setminus C) = U \cap (X \setminus C)$, an intersection of two
members of $\mathcal{T}$.

**Why the compact sets are also required to be closed.** The complement of a
compact set that is not closed in $X$ would not make $\infty$'s neighbourhoods
behave: the union computation in (T2) uses that an intersection of the discarded
sets is again closed, and the intersection of arbitrary compact subsets of a
non-Hausdorff space need not be compact. When $X$ is Hausdorff every compact
subset is closed ([[thm-compact-subset-of-a-hausdorff-space-is-closed]]) and the
two descriptions agree, which is why many texts state the definition without the
word "closed" and silently assume the Hausdorff case.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$(X^{*}, \mathcal{T}^{*})$ be its one-point compactification, with added point
$\infty$ ([[def-one-point-compactification]]). Then:

1. **$X^{*}$ is compact** ([[def-compact-space]]).
2. **$X$ is an open subspace of $X^{*}$**: $X \in \mathcal{T}^{*}$, and the
   subspace topology that $X$ inherits from $X^{*}$
   ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]) is $\mathcal{T}$ itself.
3. **$X$ is dense in $X^{*}$** ([[def-dense-top]]) **if and only if $X$ is not
   compact.**
4. **$X^{*}$ is Hausdorff** ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) **if and only if $X$ is
   locally compact** ([[def-locally-compact-space]]) **and Hausdorff.**

In particular, a locally compact Hausdorff space is an open subspace of a compact
Hausdorff space, which is the reason the construction is made. **No choice
principle is used**: the only cover thinned below is thinned by the indexed form
of [[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], which returns its own indices.

Let
$$S^2:=\{(x,y,t)\in\mathbb R^3:x^2+y^2+t^2=1\}.$$
Define
$$\Sigma(z)=\left(\frac{2\operatorname{Re}z}{1+|z|^2},\ \frac{2\operatorname{Im}z}{1+|z|^2},\ \frac{|z|^2-1}{1+|z|^2}\right)\qquad(z\in\mathbb C)$$
and $\Sigma(\infty)=(0,0,1)$. Then $\Sigma:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to S^2$ is a
homeomorphism, with inverse
$$\Pi(x,y,t)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x+iy}{1-t},&(x,y,t)\neq(0,0,1),\\ \infty,&(x,y,t)=(0,0,1).\end{cases}$$

If $f:X\to Y$ is a homotopy equivalence, then for every $n\geq 0$ and every
abelian group $G$ the induced map
$$H_n(f_\#):H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G)\to H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(Y;G)$$
is an isomorphism.

For $n\ge1$, $\widetilde H_k(S^n;G)$ is $G$ for $k=n$ and $0$ otherwise.
For $S^0$, $\widetilde H_0(S^0;G)\cong G$ and all other reduced groups vanish.
Thus $H_0(S^n;G)\cong G$ for $n\ge1$, whereas
$H_0(S^0;G)\cong G\oplus G$.

Assume AC. For every field $k$, every space $X$, and $n\ge0$, evaluation gives a natural $k$-linear isomorphism
$$H^n(X;k)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Hom}_k(H_n(X;k),k).$$
There is no finite-dimensional hypothesis. The right side is the full algebraic dual.

A morphism $f:X\to Y$ of classical varieties is projective here if there is an integer $N\ge0$ and a factorization $X\hookrightarrow Y\times\mathbf P_k^N\to Y$ in which the first map is a closed immersion and the second is projection. The product and its standard charts are supplied by [[lem-relative-projective-homogeneous-equations]]. A closed immersion in this classical setting is an isomorphism onto a reduced closed subvariety. Morphisms have the general locally ringed-space meaning of [[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]], checked on affine charts.

Work over a fixed algebraically closed field $k$, with the Axiom of Choice. Classical varieties are separated and admit finite affine covers; they may be reducible or empty unless irreducibility is specified. Irreducible means nonempty. All fibres and points below are classical closed-point fibres and points.

Assume AC. Let $f:X\to Y$ be one morphism of reduced quasi-projective complex
algebraic varieties, and prescribe finitely many closed or locally closed
algebraic subsets in source and target. There exist finite smooth complex
algebraic Whitney (a),(b) stratifications with frontier on $X$ and $Y$
respecting all prescribed subsets, such that each source stratum maps
surjectively and smoothly onto one target stratum. A further finite algebraic
stratification may be prescribed and refined. The analytic strata are smooth
complex manifolds and the restrictions are smooth submersions. If $f$ is proper
in the analytic topology, in particular if it is a projective algebraic
morphism, the whole restriction $f^{-1}(T)\to T$ over any target stratum is
proper; no restriction of $f$ to a nonclosed individual source stratum is
asserted proper.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a metric space
([[def-metric-space]]) having a neighbourhood basis of contractible open sets at
every point, and let $k$ be a field. Write $k_X$ for its constant sheaf. There
are natural isomorphisms
$$H^q(X,k_X)\cong H^q_{\operatorname{sing}}(X;k)$$
in every degree, where the left side is derived cohomology in the category of
sheaves of $k$-vector spaces (computed with the functorial $k$-linear injective
resolutions supplied by
[[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]]; compare
[[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]). The same assertion holds on
every open subset of $X$. In particular a nonempty contractible space with this
local property has constant-sheaf cohomology $k$ in degree zero and zero
otherwise. This applies to every finite-polyhedral open star and to its
nonempty intersection with a closed simplex.

derivations.claim: The space and its two charts. Let $S$ be the classical complex algebraic variety obtained by gluing two copies of the affine line $\mathbb C$, with coordinates $z$ and $w$, along the principal open subsets $z\neq0$ and $w\neq0$ by the regular isomorphism $z=1/w$; a gluing of two affine models along an open subset is a classical prevariety, and here it is separated, checked on the two charts, with the finite two-chart cover exhibiting finite type over $\mathbb C$ ([F2], [F3]). The same two charts identify $S$ with the Riemann sphere $\widehat{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}$ of [F4]: the $z$-chart is a homeomorphism onto $\mathbb C$, the $w$-chart attaches the remaining point as $\infty$, and the transition $w=1/z$ is the corresponding homeomorphism of the pointed charts; in particular $S$ is compact, since $X^*$ is compact for every space $X$ ([F4]).

The map is proper surjective. The unique morphism $f:S\to\mathrm{pt}$ is surjective because $S$ is nonempty. It is projective in the sense of [F9]: the identity is a closed immersion $S\hookrightarrow\mathrm{pt}\times\mathbb P^1(\mathbb C)$ onto a reduced closed subvariety, and the projection to the point is the structure map. By the properness clause of [F10], a projective algebraic morphism is proper in the analytic topology; hence $f$ is a proper surjective morphism of finite-type complex algebraic varieties, and [F1] applies to it.

The single fiber is not acyclic. Stereographic projection is a homeomorphism $\widehat{\mathbb C}\to S^2$ ([F5]); a homeomorphism is a homotopy equivalence, so it induces isomorphisms on singular homology ([F6]) and $H_2(S;k)\cong H_2(S^2;k)\cong k$ by [F7]. The field-dual corollary [F8] then gives $H^2(S;k)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_k(H_2(S;k),k)\cong k\neq0$, since $k$ is a field. The sphere is metric with a contractible-open neighbourhood basis, and these properties transfer through the homeomorphism, so [F11] identifies this singular cohomology group with the actual derived constant-sheaf group $H^2(S,k_S)$. Thus the fiber $S$ of $f$ is not cohomologically acyclic.

The rows are still contracted. The fiber of $f$ over the unique point is $S$ and the fiber powers are $S^{p+1}$. Choose one point $y\in S$, for instance the point with $z=0$, and for $r\geq0$ let $\mathrm{ins}_r:S^r\to S^{r+1}$ insert $y$ as first coordinate, with $S^0=\mathrm{pt}$. The deletion maps $d_i:S^{r+1}\to S^r$ satisfy $d_0\,\mathrm{ins}_{r+1}=\mathrm{id}$ and $d_i\,\mathrm{ins}_{r+1}=\mathrm{ins}_r\,d_{i-1}$ for $i>0$, so with $h_{p+1}:=\mathrm{ins}_{p+1}^*$ and $\delta_p$ the alternating sum of deletion pullbacks one gets $h_{p+1}\delta_p+\delta_{p-1}h_p=\mathrm{id}$ in every internal degree $q$, and $h_0\delta_{-1}=\mathrm{id}$; hence each augmented row is contractible. In the row $q=2$ the term at $p=0$ is $H^2(S;k)\cong k\neq0$, carried injectively into $H^2(S^2;k)$; the nonzero group is retained and does not obstruct exactness.

Conclusion. Applying [F1] to $f$ and the constant sheaf $k$, and using that the fiber powers of $f$ are $S^{p+1}$ and that $R\Gamma(\mathrm{pt},k)=k$ is concentrated in degree $0$, the augmented Cech map $k\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Tot}_{p\geq0}R\Gamma(S^{p+1},k)$ is a quasi-isomorphism; therefore the unaugmented product total has cohomology $k$ in degree $0$ and zero in every other degree. The example shows that proper Cech descent does not require acyclic fibers: the nonvanishing $H^2$ of the fiber is retained throughout the contracted rows. The Axiom of Choice is inherited through the descent lemma and the field-dual corollary, and the construction of $S$, the homeomorphism with $S^2$, the choice of one point and the insertion argument use no further choice.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as inherited from the supplied six-functor resolutions. Let $X_\bullet\to X$ be an augmented simplicial finite-type complex algebraic variety ([[def-simplicial-object-and-simplicial-commutative-ring]], [[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]). Assume $X_0\to X$ is proper surjective and, for each $p>0$, $X_p\to(\operatorname{cosk}_{p-1}\operatorname{sk}_{p-1}X_\bullet)_p$ is proper surjective over $X$, where skeleton and coskeleton are the standard finite-limit constructions of the simplicial category and the target is the matching object. Such an object is a proper hypercover; no smoothness or fiber acyclicity is assumed. For $F\in D^b_c(X;k)$ over a field, and $a_p:X_p\to X$, the augmentation gives
$$F\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Tot}_{p\geq0}Ra_{p*}a_p^*F,\qquad R\Gamma(X,F)\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Tot}_{p\geq0}R\Gamma(X_p,a_p^*F).$$
There is a natural strongly convergent spectral sequence $E_1^{p,q}=H^q(X_p,a_p^*F)\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(X,F)$. If $F$ has cochain lower bound $a$, every diagonal $p+q=m$ is finite; degree $m$ and its differential are determined by levels through $p=m-a+1$. All proper-hypercover refinements induce the same comparison via the base object; any two such hypercovers have a proper common refinement. For $F=k_X$, $a=0$, this is the first-quadrant spectral sequence required for smooth-projective hyperresolutions.

Let $\Delta$ be the **simplex category**: its objects are the finite nonempty
ordered sets $[n]=\{0<1<\dots<n\}$ for $n\ge0$, and its morphisms are the
order-preserving maps. A **simplicial object** in a category $\mathcal C$ is a
functor $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathcal C$
([[def-category]], [[def-functor-and-contravariant-functor]]). A **simplicial
set** is a simplicial object in sets; a **simplicial commutative ring** is a
simplicial object in commutative rings ([[def-commutative-ring]]), so that
each $A_n$ is a commutative ring and the structure maps are ring
homomorphisms ([[def-ring-homomorphism]]); a **simplicial module** over a
simplicial ring $A_\bullet$ is a simplicial object $M_\bullet$ in abelian
groups together with a compatible $A_\bullet$-action, and the resulting
category of simplicial $A_\bullet$-modules is abelian.

Writing $d_i\colon M_n\to M_{n-1}$ for the image of the injection
$[n-1]\to[n]$ omitting $i$ (a **face map**) and $s_i\colon M_n\to M_{n+1}$
for the image of the surjection $[n+1]\to[n]$ repeating $i$ (a **degeneracy
map**), these maps satisfy the usual simplicial identities
$$d_i d_j=d_{j-1}d_i\ (i<j),\qquad s_i s_j=s_{j+1}s_i\ (i\le j),\qquad d_i s_j=\begin{cases} s_{j-1}d_i, & i<j,\\ \mathrm{id}, & i=j\ \text{or}\ i=j+1,\\ s_j d_{i-1}, & i>j+1.\end{cases}$$
Conversely, such a sequence of face and degeneracy maps determines the
functor.

The **Moore complex** of a simplicial abelian group or module $M_\bullet$ is
the chain complex concentrated in nonnegative degrees with $M_n$ in degree
$n$ and differential
$$\partial_n=\sum_{i=0}^{n}(-1)^i d_i\colon M_n\to M_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1),$$
with $\partial_0=0$; the $d_i$ are the face maps
([[def-chain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]]);
the simplicial identities give $\partial_{n-1}\partial_n=0$. Its homology is
written
$$\pi_n(M_\bullet)=H_n(M_\bullet)\qquad(n\ge0)$$
([[def-homology-object-of-a-chain-complex]]). By the Dold-Kan normalization
theorem this agrees with the classical homotopy-group definition
$H_n(NM_\bullet)$ via the normalized subcomplex, so the convention is
canonical; no model-category machinery is introduced here.

For a simplicial commutative ring $A_\bullet$, each $\pi_n(A_\bullet)$ is defined as above, and $\pi_0(A_\bullet)=A_0/(d_0-d_1)(A_1)$ is a commutative ring. The image is an ideal: for $a\in A_0$, multiplying a representative $b\in A_1$ by $s_0a$ gives $a(d_0b-d_1b)$. Every $\pi_n(A_\bullet)$ is a $\pi_0(A_\bullet)$-module. Indeed multiplication by the totally degenerate simplex of a vertex $a\in A_0$ is a chain map on the Moore complex: its faces are the corresponding totally degenerate simplex of $a$ in the preceding degree. If two vertices are the endpoints of $b\in A_1$, multiplication by the simplicial path defined by $b$ gives a homotopy between these chain maps (the alternating prism sum inserts the degeneracies of $b$). Consequently $(d_0-d_1)(b)$ acts as zero on homology, so the action factors through the displayed quotient. Additivity, associativity and the unit descend from levelwise ring multiplication.

A **morphism of simplicial commutative rings** is a natural transformation
$A_\bullet\to B_\bullet$ ([[def-natural-transformation]]). Such a morphism is
a **weak equivalence** when it induces isomorphisms
$\pi_n(A_\bullet)\to\pi_n(B_\bullet)$ for all $n\ge0$. The **category of
derived rings** is the localization of the category of simplicial commutative
rings at the weak equivalences; constructions on derived rings are used below
only through statements that are independent of the chosen replacement up to
canonical isomorphism.

derivations.claim: Degree bookkeeping. In the total complex of the hypercover, the term in bidegree $(p,q)$ has $p\geq0$ and $q\geq a$ and contributes to total degree $p+q$. For a fixed total degree $m$ this gives $0\leq p\leq m-a$. The differentials entering and leaving total degree $m$ involve terms of total degree $m-1$, $m$ and $m+1$, so the largest simplicial level appearing in the data of $H^m$ and of its differential is $p=(m+1)-a=m-a+1$.

The truncation computes the same cohomology. By [F1], the comparison of $X_\bullet$ with its $N$-coskeleton truncation $\operatorname{cosk}_N\operatorname{sk}_NX_\bullet$ is the identity through simplicial degree $N$, and the total complex in a fixed total degree uses only finitely many levels. Choosing $N\geq m-a+1$ makes the two total complexes agree in degrees $m-1$, $m$ and $m+1$; hence they have the same $H^m$ and the same augmentation maps there. Since $m$ was arbitrary, every truncation with $N$ at least the stated bound computes the same cohomology $H^m(X,F)$.

Constant coefficients and sharpness for hard truncation. For $F=k_X$ the lower bound is $a=0$, so the actual total-degree computation uses the outgoing map from level $n$ to level $n+1$. To see that omitting that map can change the answer in every degree, take the proper surjection from two reduced points $S=\{0,1\}$ to a point and its Cech nerve. The normalized degree-$p$ cochains are $k^2$, indexed by the two alternating nondegenerate strings of length $p+1$. Interior deletions give degenerate strings and vanish in the normalized differential; the two endpoint deletions give $\delta_p(v_0,v_1)=(v_1+(-1)^{p+1}v_0,v_0+(-1)^{p+1}v_1)$, which has rank one over every field. The full augmented complex is contracted by inserting one point, as in [F1], so its positive cohomology is zero and $H^0=k$. If one retains only cochain levels $0,\ldots,n$ and discards $\delta_n$, its top cohomology is $k$ for $n>0$ and $k^2$ for $n=0$, giving the wrong answer. Thus level $n+1$ is necessary in general for this hard truncation of the cochain data. A coskeleton truncation is different: it reconstructs higher levels from matching limits, so no claim that $\operatorname{cosk}_n\operatorname{sk}_nX_\bullet$ itself fails descent is made.
